I should look more carefully at whether evidence passages E7, E8, E9 (referenced in numeric_checks but not provided in the original evidence list) contain the December 31, 2025 figure, or whether the system is comparing to the wrong period. If the December 31, 2025 figure exists in the evidence, my verdict of INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE would be wrong.

This suggests there may be additional evidence containing the actual balance sheet figures that I did not review. If those passages contain both the December 31, 2025 and September 30, 2026 long-term debt balances, and show that September 30, 2026 was indeed higher, then the claim should be SUPPORTED rather than INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE.

Even with the evidence provided (E1-E6), I may have missed relevant information. Evidence E1 and E2 describe substantial debt issuances totaling approximately $80.8 billion during 2026 ($45.0B USD + $35.8B foreign currency). If the starting long-term debt at December 31, 2025 was relatively low and these issuances were not offset by significant repayments, this would strongly support the claim. I should have considered whether the qualitative evidence about issuances, combined with any balance sheet data that might be embedded in the evidence passages, could verify the claim.
